title: Social loafing
text: People working in groups sometimes put in less effort than they would alone. This tendency is known as social loafing. It appears most often when individual contributions are hard to identify. For example, members of a team pulling a rope each pull less hard as more people join. Researchers believe that people feel less responsible when their work cannot be measured. However, the effect becomes smaller when each person's role is clearly defined and the task feels meaningful.

title: Peer tutoring
text: Peer tutoring is an approach in which students help classmates learn new material. The tutor usually explains a concept, asks questions, and checks the partner's understanding. Studies show that both partners often benefit from these sessions. The learner receives personal attention, while the tutor must organize knowledge clearly in order to teach it. For instance, older students who tutor younger ones frequently improve their own reading skills. However, tutors need some training, or they may simply give answers instead of guiding thinking.

title: Opportunity cost
text: Every economic choice involves giving up something else of value. Economists call the value of the best alternative not chosen the opportunity cost. For example, a student who spends an evening working at a cafe loses time that could have been used for studying. The cost is not only money but also time and other possible benefits. Thinking about these hidden costs can lead to better decisions. However, people often overlook them because they are less visible than prices.

title: Customer loyalty programs
text: Many stores reward customers who return to buy again. These loyalty programs usually give points or discounts after a certain number of purchases. The main goal is to make switching to a competitor feel less attractive. A coffee shop, for example, might offer a free drink after ten visits. Such programs also help companies collect information about buying habits. However, if every competitor offers similar rewards, the advantage for any single store becomes quite small.

title: Agenda setting by news media
text: News media influence not only what people think but also what they think about. This idea is called agenda setting. When newspapers and broadcasts give a topic frequent coverage, audiences begin to see it as important. For example, a series of reports on road safety can make citizens rank traffic problems as a major public concern. The media do not fully control opinions, however. People also rely on personal experience and conversations with friends when judging which issues matter.

title: Mixed-use neighborhoods
text: Some cities encourage neighborhoods that combine homes, shops, and offices in the same area. In these mixed districts, residents can walk to many daily destinations instead of driving. Streets also stay busy at different times of day, which may make them feel safer. For example, a small grocery store on the ground floor of an apartment building serves people living upstairs. However, planners must manage noise and delivery traffic so that residents remain comfortable.

title: Handwashing and infection
text: Washing hands with soap is one of the simplest ways to prevent disease. Soap breaks down the oily layer that surrounds many germs, and rinsing carries them away. Hospitals that improved handwashing routines have reported fewer infections among patients. Schools have seen similar results, with fewer student absences during cold and flu seasons. The practice works best when people wash for long enough and dry their hands properly. However, reminders are often needed because habits tend to slip over time.

title: Two-step verification
text: Many online accounts now ask users to confirm their identity in two different ways. After entering a password, a person may need to type a short code sent to a phone. This extra step protects the account even if the password has been stolen. An attacker would also need physical access to the phone. As a result, the method greatly reduces unauthorized logins. However, users can lose access themselves if they change phones without updating their settings.

title: Sleep and learning
text: Sleep plays an important role in turning new information into lasting memories. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay and strengthen patterns formed during the day. Students who sleep well after studying usually remember more than those who stay awake all night. For example, learners tested the morning after practicing a list of words often recall more of them. However, sleep cannot replace study itself. It mainly helps protect material that was already learned.

title: The bystander effect
text: People are often less likely to help in an emergency when many others are present. Psychologists call this pattern the bystander effect. Each person may assume that someone else will act or has already called for help. Uncertainty also plays a role, since onlookers watch one another to decide whether the situation is serious. In experiments, participants responded faster when they believed they were alone. However, the effect weakens when a person is directly asked to help.

title: Inflation and savings
text: Inflation is a general rise in prices across an economy over time. When prices increase, each unit of money buys fewer goods than before. This change affects people who keep their savings in cash. For example, money hidden at home for several years may purchase noticeably less when it is finally spent. Savers often choose accounts that pay interest to protect their purchasing power. However, if interest rates stay below inflation, savings still lose value.

title: Remote work
text: Remote work allows employees to do their jobs from home instead of an office. Supporters argue that it saves commuting time and gives workers more control over their schedules. Some companies have also reduced spending on office space. However, working apart can make spontaneous conversations less common. New employees in particular may find it harder to learn informal rules and build relationships. For this reason, many organizations now combine remote days with regular meetings in person.

title: Libraries as community spaces
text: Public libraries have changed from places mainly for borrowing books into broad community centers. Many now offer free internet access, job search help, and language classes. For people without computers at home, these services can be essential. Libraries also provide quiet study areas for students who lack space elsewhere. Because they are open to everyone, they bring together residents of different ages and backgrounds. However, these expanded roles require funding that is not always guaranteed.

title: Satellite navigation
text: Satellite navigation helps drivers find routes in unfamiliar places. A receiver in the phone or car measures signals from several satellites. By comparing how long each signal takes to arrive, it calculates its own position. The system then matches this position to a digital map and suggests a route. Some apps also use reports from other users to avoid traffic jams. However, signals can weaken between tall buildings, so the displayed location is sometimes slightly wrong.

title: Herd immunity
text: Vaccines protect not only the people who receive them but also their communities. When a large share of a population is immune, a disease has fewer chances to spread. This indirect protection is called herd immunity. It helps people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies or patients with weak immune systems. The share of people needed depends on how contagious the disease is. However, protection can fade if vaccination rates fall over time.

title: Cognitive dissonance
text: When people hold beliefs that conflict with their actions, they often experience psychological discomfort. Psychologists refer to this state as cognitive dissonance. To reduce it, individuals frequently adjust their attitudes rather than change their behavior. In a classic experiment, participants who were paid only a small amount to describe a boring task as enjoyable subsequently rated the task more favorably than those who were paid generously. Presumably, the smaller payment provided insufficient justification, so participants altered their opinions instead. Nevertheless, the strength of this effect varies considerably across cultures and situations.

title: Anchoring in negotiation
text: The first number mentioned in a negotiation can strongly shape the final agreement. This tendency, known as anchoring, occurs because people adjust insufficiently from an initial reference point. Consequently, a seller who opens with a high asking price often secures a higher final price, even when buyers recognize the opening offer as excessive. Experiments have demonstrated that even arbitrary numbers can influence estimates of value. Experienced negotiators therefore prepare their own reference points in advance. However, an extreme opening offer may be perceived as unreasonable and can damage trust between the parties.

title: Moral hazard
text: Insurance can unintentionally change the behavior of the people it protects. Economists describe this problem as moral hazard. Once individuals are protected against losses, they may have less incentive to avoid risky behavior. For instance, a driver with comprehensive coverage might be somewhat less careful about locking the car. Insurers therefore introduce deductibles, which require policyholders to pay part of any loss themselves. This arrangement ensures that customers retain a financial interest in preventing damage. Nevertheless, excessively high deductibles may discourage people from purchasing adequate coverage at all.

title: Diffusion of innovations
text: New technologies rarely spread through a society at a constant rate. Instead, adoption typically begins slowly, accelerates rapidly, and eventually levels off. A small group of innovators adopts first, followed by early adopters whose opinions are respected by others. Once these individuals demonstrate the benefits, the majority subsequently follows. Adoption is predominantly influenced by whether an innovation is compatible with existing habits and whether its advantages are easily observed. However, some potential users may continue to resist for economic or cultural reasons.

title: Gentrification
text: Gentrification refers to the process by which wealthier residents move into historically lower-income neighborhoods. As demand for housing increases, property values and rents typically rise. Consequently, residents who have lived there for decades may be unable to afford to stay. New investment can improve infrastructure, commercial services, and public safety. However, the original community frequently loses its social networks and cultural character. Researchers continue to debate whether displacement is as widespread as commonly assumed, since outcomes vary considerably between cities and depend heavily on local housing policies.

title: Social determinants of health
text: Health is shaped not only by medical care but also by the conditions in which people live and work. Public health researchers refer to these factors as social determinants of health. They include income, education, housing quality, and access to nutritious food. For example, residents of neighborhoods with few grocery stores are predominantly dependent on processed foods, which increases the risk of chronic disease. Consequently, improving health outcomes may require policies beyond the hospital. However, isolating the effect of any single factor is difficult, because these conditions are closely interrelated.

title: Recommendation algorithms
text: Online platforms use recommendation systems to predict which content each user will find appealing. These algorithms analyze previous behavior, such as clicks and viewing time, and compare it with the behavior of similar users. Items that are predicted to be engaging are subsequently displayed more prominently. Although this approach helps users navigate enormous collections, critics argue that it may gradually narrow the range of viewpoints people encounter. Because popular content receives additional exposure, it tends to become even more popular. However, empirical evidence regarding the strength of this narrowing effect remains mixed.

title: Formative assessment
text: Not all classroom assessment is intended to produce a final grade. Formative assessment is conducted during instruction so that teachers can identify misunderstandings while there is still time to address them. Brief quizzes, exit questions, and peer feedback are commonly used for this purpose. Students who receive specific comments, rather than merely scores, are generally more likely to improve subsequent work. Consequently, the information gathered is used to adjust teaching rather than to rank learners. Nevertheless, the approach requires considerable time, which may be limited in crowded classrooms.

title: Comparative advantage
text: Countries can benefit from trade even when one of them produces everything more efficiently. According to the principle of comparative advantage, each country should specialize in goods it produces at the lowest opportunity cost. If a nation exports such goods and imports others, total output across both partners increases. For example, a country with abundant farmland might concentrate on agriculture, while a neighbor with skilled engineers focuses on machinery. Both can subsequently consume more than they could produce independently. However, the gains are not distributed evenly, and workers in declining industries may experience considerable hardship.

title: Owners and managers
text: When owners hire managers to run a company, their interests may not perfectly align. Shareholders, who act as principals, want the firm to grow in value over many years, whereas managers, acting as agents, may prefer higher salaries or less demanding work. Because owners cannot observe every decision, managers have considerable freedom. To address this problem, firms frequently tie executive pay to company performance. Nevertheless, such incentives can encourage managers to focus excessively on results that are easily measured.

title: Two-step flow of communication
text: Early researchers assumed that mass media influenced audiences directly and powerfully. Later studies, however, suggested that messages are often transmitted in two stages. Information first reaches opinion leaders, who are particularly attentive to media coverage. These individuals subsequently interpret the messages and pass them on to friends, relatives, and coworkers through conversation. Consequently, personal networks can either strengthen or weaken the impact of a campaign. Although digital platforms have complicated this model, the central insight that interpersonal relationships shape persuasion remains widely accepted.

title: Induced traffic demand
text: Building additional road lanes does not always reduce traffic congestion in the long run. When a highway is widened, driving initially becomes faster and more convenient. Consequently, people who previously avoided the route, traveled at other times, or used public transport begin to drive on it. Within several years, congestion frequently returns to its former level. This phenomenon is known as induced demand. Transportation planners therefore increasingly consider alternatives such as improved transit or road pricing, although these measures are often difficult to introduce.

title: Video compression
text: Streaming a film over the internet would require enormous amounts of data without compression. Video compression algorithms reduce file size by removing information that viewers are unlikely to notice. Because consecutive frames are often nearly identical, the encoder stores only the differences between them rather than every complete image. Fine details that the human eye perceives poorly are also simplified. Consequently, a movie can be delivered smoothly over an ordinary home connection. However, when the available bandwidth is insufficient, the system lowers quality, and viewers may notice blurred or blocky images.

title: Sunk cost fallacy
text: Rational decisions should depend on future costs and benefits rather than on past expenses. Nevertheless, people frequently continue an activity simply because they have already invested money, time, or effort in it. This tendency is known as the sunk cost fallacy. For example, a company may keep funding an unsuccessful project because abandoning it would seem to waste previous spending. Such reasoning is understandable, since admitting a mistake can be uncomfortable. However, resources that cannot be recovered should not determine whether additional resources are committed.

title: Placebo effect
text: Patients sometimes improve after receiving a treatment that contains no active ingredient. This phenomenon, known as the placebo effect, is predominantly attributed to expectation and conditioning. When individuals believe that a treatment will help, their perception of symptoms such as pain may genuinely change. For this reason, new medicines are typically compared with placebos in controlled trials, where neither patients nor researchers know who receives which treatment. However, placebos rarely cure underlying diseases, and their effects are generally strongest for subjective symptoms.
